chapters.name: Signs, Signals, and Pavement Markings
chapters.summary: What sign shapes and colors mean, how to respond to steady and flashing lights and arrows, and what yellow and white lines on the road tell you.
keyPoints: Red signs mean stop, yield, or do not enter. Yellow means warning, orange means road work, and white means a rule you must obey.
The white X-shaped crossbuck marks a railroad crossing. Treat it like a yield sign.
A flashing red light means the same as a STOP sign. A flashing yellow light means slow down and go with care.
Yellow lines separate traffic going in opposite directions. White lines separate lanes going the same way.

chapters.name: Right of Way and Intersections
chapters.summary: Who goes first at stop signs, four-way stops, uncontrolled intersections, and turns, and how to yield to pedestrians, emergency vehicles, school buses, and trains.
keyPoints: At a four-way stop, the first to arrive goes first. If two arrive together, the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right.
Stop for a school bus with red lights flashing and stop arm out. On a highway with 4 or more lanes, traffic going the other way does not have to stop.
Under Scott's Law, move over or slow down for a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing lights.

chapters.name: Speed, Passing, and Parking
chapters.summary: Illinois speed limits, signaling before turns, when you may pass, and the places where you may not park.
keyPoints: When no limit is posted, the limit is 30 mph in an urban district, 15 mph in an alley, and 55 mph on most other roads.
In a school zone, the limit is 20 mph on school days when children are present.
Do not park within 15 feet of a fire hydrant, 20 feet of a crosswalk, 30 feet of a stop sign, or 50 feet of a railroad crossing.

chapters.name: Safe Driving
chapters.summary: Signaling, headlights, following distance, bad weather, work zones, sharing the road, and distracted driving.
keyPoints: Signal at least 100 feet before turning in a business or residence district, and at least 200 feet elsewhere.
Turn on headlights from sunset to sunrise and whenever rain, snow, or fog makes you use your windshield wipers.
Dim high beams within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle and within 300 feet of a vehicle you follow.

chapters.name: Instruction Permit and Teen Licensing
chapters.summary: How the instruction permit works, the supervised practice hours, and the night and passenger limits for young drivers.
keyPoints: Drivers under 18 must hold the permit at least 9 months and log 50 hours, including 10 at night.
Drivers under 18 may not drive Sunday to Thursday from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m., or Friday and Saturday from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m.
Drivers under 19 may not use a cell phone while driving, even hands-free, except in an emergency.

chapters.name: Alcohol and Drug Laws
chapters.summary: Illinois blood alcohol limits, the zero tolerance law for drivers under 21, implied consent, and how alcohol and drugs affect driving.
keyPoints: A driver 21 or older with a BAC of 0.08% or more is legally under the influence.
Under zero tolerance, a driver under 21 with any trace of alcohol loses driving privileges.
For an adult first offender, refusing a chemical test brings a 12-month suspension, and failing it brings a 6-month suspension.
